segments.text: In this video, we are looking at one of
the most practical patterns in FastAPI,
dependencies that use yield. If you have
ever needed to open a database session
before a request and reliably close it
afterward, even when something goes
wrong, this is the feature built exactly
for that job.
Imagine every route that touches your
database needs to open a session, do its
work, and then close the session whether
or not an error occurred. Without a
clean solution, you end up writing a try
finally block in every single handler.
That is repetitive, easy to forget, and
when you forget it, you get leaked
connections that silently pile up until
your database runs out of capacity.
Think about a library checkout desk. The
librarian handles the paperwork before
you take the book and again when you
return it, regardless of whether your
visit was successful or cut short. You,
the reader, just focus on reading.
A yield dependency plays the role of
that librarian. It sets up the resource,
passes it to your code, and then cleans
it up once your code is done.
A yield dependency is just a regular
Python generator function that you
register with FastAPI's depends
mechanism. Everything you write before
the yield statement is the setup phase.
FastAPI runs it, takes whatever you
yielded, and injects it into your route.
Everything after the yield is the
teardown phase, and FastAPI guarantees
it runs after the response leaves, even
if an exception was raised inside the
route.
Let's walk through this.
We create a SQL Alchemy session local
factory at the top. Then comes the
dependency function get underscore db.
It opens a fresh database session and
enters a try block. The yield statement
pauses get underscore db and hands the
open session to whoever depends on it.
In this case, the route rate underscore
item, which receives it as the parameter
db. When the route finishes, FastAPI
resumes get underscore db past the
yield, and the finally block runs
db.close, guaranteed whether the route
succeeded or raised an HTTP exception.
Internally, FastAPI uses Python's
contextlib.contextmanager machinery to
turn your generator function into a
context manager. When a request arrives,
FastAPI resolves dependencies in order,
running everything up to each yield.
Your route function executes with the
injected values. Once the response is
built and sent, FastAPI exits each
context manager in reverse order, so
tear down always fires. This means you
get the safety of try finally without
writing it yourself in every route.
Use yield dependencies whenever your
code needs to release something after
the route finishes, database sessions,
file handles, transaction contexts. The
rule of thumb is, if tear down is
required, yield belongs there. Skip it
when you are just computing or reading a
value. A plain return is simpler, and a
future reader will thank you for not
adding generator machinery where none is
needed.
To summarize, a yield dependency splits
into two phases, setup before the yield
and tear down after. FastAPI wraps this
in an implicit finally block, so cleanup
never gets skipped. This pattern is the
standard way to manage database sessions
in FastAPI, and it composes cleanly with
all of FastAPI's other dependency
features. When no tear down is needed,
stick with a regular return and keep
your code as straightforward as
possible.
